content: On an early Earth exposed to intense ultraviolet radiation, the evolution of DNA may have depended on an unexpected molecular advantage. Early life on Earth faced intense ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun without the protection of an ozone layer. Yet DNA came to rely on thymine, a chemical building block that is more prone to UV damage than uracil, its counterpart in single-stranded RNA. A study at Texas A&M University suggests that thymine may have helped early genetic molecules survive by directing that damage into a form that was easier to reverse. The findings, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), offer a possible explanation for why thymine replaced uracil as genetic systems evolved toward DNA. Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, and his research assistants, Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar, compared thymine and uracil under controlled UV conditions designed to mimic the intense radiation environment of primordial Earth. They used biophotonics, a field that applies light-based methods to biological questions. Their tools included absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy, which examine how molecules absorb, emit, or scatter light. “We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair,” said Khosh Abady. “In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule.” Rentzepis and his team plan to extend their investigation to an earlier stage in the origin-of-life process by examining the forces that brought thymine, uracil, and other components of early genetic systems together. “We hope to explore whether life’s chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems,” said Khosh Abady. “We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life’s origins.” The measurements also establish a new reference framework that could support research beyond molecular evolution. The team identified distinct spectral signatures, recognizable patterns in how the molecules interact with light, that may eventually have practical uses. “The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems,” said Khosh Abady. Reference: “UV photodamage pathways and the evolutionary selection of thymine over uracil in early genetic systems” by Keyvan Khosh Abady, Negar Karpourazar and Peter M. Rentzepis, 3 August 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2615278123 This study was supported by Air Force Office of Scientific Research Grant number FA9550-20-1-0139 and Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station funds. content: Salk Institute researchers have created a molecular map of how healthy mice respond to exercise, offering clues that could help improve performance and reduce injury risk. Exercise can help the body resist disease and dysfunction and recover from illness. Studies have also linked it to more than 30 percent lower mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Explaining those benefits is harder, partly because studies in people generally rely on blood and muscle samples, leaving researchers with an incomplete picture of how exercise changes other organs. Researchers at the Salk Institute turned to mice to follow those changes through more of the body. They compared young male and female mice that ran voluntarily on a wheel for eight weeks with mice that remained sedentary, creating a first-of-its-kind molecular atlas spanning 22 tissues. The study was published in Cell on October 15, 2026. Exercise altered the activity of nearly half the genes examined in at least one tissue, yet no single gene’s activity changed in all 22. Those comparisons came from bulk RNA sequencing, which measures gene activity across whole tissue samples. Rather than revealing one response shared everywhere, the analysis showed that tissues adapted in different ways. The researchers also cataloged the small molecules that cells use and produce during metabolism in eight tissues and plasma, the liquid part of blood. Alongside this metabolomics analysis, they used proteomics to measure protein levels in four specific leg muscles, examining a hamstring muscle, two calf muscles, and the quadriceps. “Exercise doesn’t just change our muscles, it changes many of our organs and cells at different levels—some short-term, some long-term,” says co-first and co-corresponding author Geraldine Maier, PhD, a staff scientist at Salk. “Our experimental setup allows us to capture that detail across tissues, and sexes, and in muscle, down to the individual cell types.” Skeletal muscle accounted for most of the changes in gene activity, and the strong responses in leg muscles prompted the researchers to examine three of them more closely. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, they could distinguish neighboring cell types and compare their gene activity instead of averaging their responses together. They also conducted the first single-cell analysis of DNA methylation in muscle after exercise. In some muscle cell types, training changed chemical marks on DNA that help regulate gene activity, while other cell types showed no such changes. These marks are added through a process called DNA methylation. Changes in their pattern can be more persistent than shifts in RNA or protein levels, allowing this form of epigenetic regulation to have lasting effects on how particular cell types and whole tissues behave. “Exercise impacts the whole body, not just your muscles, so an atlas like ours that looks more holistically at many tissues is key to understanding the true impact of exercise,” says co-first author Manoj Hariharan, PhD, a former senior staff scientist at Salk. “That’s also why single-cell studies are so important—there are so many cell type-specific changes that get lost in bulk sequencing. I hope our work highlights that and encourages more single-cell atlases, and especially multi-omic single-cell atlases, moving forward.” Female mice showed broader changes in gene activity and distinct expression patterns compared with males. The epigenetic response to training also differed strongly by sex. To capture variation across daily biological rhythms, the researchers collected tissues during both the active and resting phases of the mice’s circadian cycle. Most tissues showed greater exercise-related changes when sampled during the active phase, with the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung as exceptions. “Our atlas provides a comprehensive resource for understanding the systemic molecular adaptations to endurance exercise,” says co-first author Ramesh Ramasamy, PhD, a former computational biologist at Salk. “Now that we have all this data, researchers can begin developing strategies that harness exercise—either alone or in combination with other interventions—to ensure we all live long, healthy lives.” The researchers have already used the gene activity dataset to develop a 51-gene exercise signature, a pattern that distinguishes exercise-trained muscle from sedentary muscle in both mice and humans. It could help identify biomarkers, measurable indicators of a biological state, and support research into muscle disuse and dysfunction. By establishing a healthy baseline, the atlas gives researchers a reference for investigating how tissues adapt to exercise. The differences by sex and circadian phase could eventually inform more personalized exercise routines, while closer investigation of particular tissues and cell types may point to ways of improving performance, recovery, and muscle health. “Now that we have the data,” adds Maier, “labs can identify one gene or metabolic pathway they find interesting, then dissect that mechanism. Our atlas gives the field a shared foundation to build on.” How long those molecular changes last remains unresolved. Researchers still need to determine how long training must continue before lasting changes develop and whether cells retain a memory of exercise for months or years. Reference: “Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise” by Geraldine Maier, Manoj Hariharan, Ramesh K. Ramasamy, Aidan Glina, Laura van Rosmalen, Suraj J. title: Car buyers are demanding lower prices and better tech. Automakers must deliver both
content: Global automakers face an increasingly demanding customer: one who wants both competitive prices and better technology, according to Bain & Company. Tech and features were a leading purchase consideration for 58% of Chinese consumers, ranking ahead of price, the consultancy's latest Global Automotive Consumer Survey found. In the U.S. and Europe, price remained the top consideration, cited by 68% and 62%, respectively. However, that does not mean Chinese buyers have stopped caring about affordability. Intense domestic competition has made low prices an expectation in China, pushing carmakers to stand out through technology and features, Bain executives told CNBC. Stricker expects Western markets to follow, with competitive pricing becoming a baseline and technology playing a bigger role in purchasing decisions. Moreover, growing competition from Chinese manufacturers is expected to intensify pricing pressure in Europe, he added. China’s vehicle exports to Italy more than doubled to 209,258 units in January-August, while U.K. shipments rose about 86% to 365,672, according to customs figures cited by the China Passenger Car Association . Meanwhile, weakening brand loyalty threatens an advantage established manufacturers have relied on for decades. "European manufacturers [have] basically based their business model for decades on brand loyalty," Stricker said, but that allegiance is fading. More than a third of customers in Western markets are open to new brands entering the market, Bain's survey found. Buyers most interested in autonomous-driving technology are also more willing to switch manufacturers for better functionality. Helen Liu, Asia automotive head and partner at Bain, said that younger U.S. and European consumers are closer to Chinese buyers in their openness to technology, adding that Western manufacturers need to "up their game" to retain those customers. But monetizing those features could prove difficult. While Stricker said that mass-market buyers often expected advanced driving technology to be included rather than carry a substantial premium, Liu added that those demands leave Chinese and Western manufacturers "climbing different mountains." Emerging Chinese players must build their brand standing, while Western incumbents must strengthen their technology offerings. All players must keep prices competitive. Manufacturers that can close their respective gaps without pricing themselves out of buyers' consideration stand to gain the most as the industry consolidates , according to Bain. – CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this story.
